Model Predictive Path Integral Control

The preceding chapters formulated deterministic trajectory optimization as a nonlinear program. Shooting and collocation turn the dynamics, costs, and constraints into a finite-dimensional problem that we can solve with an NLP solver. Gradient-based methods are effective when accurate derivatives are available. How can we improve a trajectory when we can simulate the system and evaluate its cost, but differentiating through that computation is difficult or expensive?

Model predictive path integral control (MPPI) uses sampling to construct an update. It draws candidate control sequences, simulates their trajectories, and forms a weighted average that favors lower-cost outcomes. This requires no derivatives of the dynamics or cost, and the candidate rollouts can run in parallel. The derivation begins with a distribution over control sequences: costs determine which sequences receive more probability, and fitting a Gaussian to that distribution gives the weighted-average update. This construction applies even to a deterministic simulator. An aircraft example extends the calculation to uncertain winds by estimating each candidate flight’s expected cost before assigning its weight. Executing the first action and planning again from the next observation connects these computations to the following chapter on receding-horizon control.

Learning Goals¶

After working through the examples and exercises, you should be able to:

  • Calculate an MPPI update, including the correction for sampling around a nonzero nominal control sequence.

  • Derive exponential weighting from a KL-regularized objective and obtain the control update by fitting a Gaussian mean.

  • Distinguish samples used to explore controls from samples used to estimate a candidate’s expected cost under physical disturbances.

  • Assess a sampled plan using feasibility checks, weight concentration, and comparisons under shared disturbances.

  • Execute the first action of a sampled plan and update the remaining plan from new observations.

Prerequisites¶

The algorithm uses the single-shooting rollout and the finite-horizon optimal-control formulation. The sampling derivation requires Gaussian distributions and expectations; KL divergence and importance sampling are developed here. The aircraft example uses conditional disturbance models from Stochastic Dynamics and Partial Observation.

Improving a Control Sequence by Sampling¶

We already know how to evaluate a control sequence: simulate the system and compute the resulting cost. How can we improve that sequence? Instead of computing a gradient, we try many random variations, evaluate each one, and form a weighted average that gives more influence to the lower-cost candidates. That average becomes our next control sequence.

If the system has dud_udu​ control components, then uk∈Rdu\mathbf u_k\in\mathbb R^{d_u}uk​∈Rdu​ contains the inputs applied together at time step kkk. The current plan U=(u0,…,uN−1)\mathbf U=(\mathbf u_0,\ldots,\mathbf u_{N-1})U=(u0​,…,uN−1​) collects these vectors over all NNN steps. Thus uk\mathbf u_kuk​ is one step’s control vector, while U\mathbf UU is the complete sequence, with NduNd_uNdu​ entries when stacked into one vector.

Draw KKK Gaussian perturbation sequences ϵ(i)\boldsymbol\epsilon^{(i)}ϵ(i) and simulate each candidate V(i)=U+ϵ(i)\mathbf V^{(i)}=\mathbf U+\boldsymbol\epsilon^{(i)}V(i)=U+ϵ(i). After assigning normalized weights wiw_iwi​ to the resulting trajectories, form the new control sequence

U+=∑i=1KwiV(i)=U+∑i=1Kwiϵ(i),wi≥0,∑i=1Kwi=1.\mathbf U^+=\sum_{i=1}^K w_i\mathbf V^{(i)} =\mathbf U+\sum_{i=1}^K w_i\boldsymbol\epsilon^{(i)}, \qquad w_i\geq0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^K w_i=1.U+=i=1∑K​wi​V(i)=U+i=1∑K​wi​ϵ(i),wi​≥0,i=1∑K​wi​=1.
(1)

The same trajectory weight multiplies every action in its sequence. How should those weights depend on the costs? Giving every candidate the same weight, wi=1/Kw_i=1/Kwi​=1/K, would ignore the rollout results. Because the perturbations have mean zero, this update would return U\mathbf UU on average, regardless of which candidates performed well. At the other extreme, assigning weight one to the lowest-cost candidate and zero to the others would select a single sequence. A candidate with a nearly identical cost would have no influence, and a small change in which candidate ranks first could switch the entire update.

MPPI allows several low-cost candidates to contribute, with their influence decreasing smoothly as cost increases. Consider first the initial sequence U=0\mathbf U=\mathbf0U=0. The candidate sequences are then the zero-mean Gaussian perturbations themselves. This Gaussian is the reference distribution: it remains fixed even when later updates move the sampling mean away from zero. Let SiS_iSi​ be the accumulated state cost along rollout iii, including its terminal cost. MPPI assigns it the positive score exp⁡(−Si/λ)\exp(-S_i/\lambda)exp(−Si​/λ) and divides by the sum of all scores:

wi=exp⁡(−Si/λ)∑j=1Kexp⁡(−Sj/λ),λ>0.w_i=\frac{\exp(-S_i/\lambda)}{\sum_{j=1}^K\exp(-S_j/\lambda)}, \qquad \lambda>0.wi​=∑j=1K​exp(−Sj​/λ)exp(−Si​/λ)​,λ>0.
(2)

This is the softmax of the negative costs, with temperature λ\lambdaλ. The minus sign makes lower costs receive larger scores, and the denominator makes the weights sum to one. The parameter λ\lambdaλ has the same units as cost, so Si/λS_i/\lambdaSi​/λ is dimensionless. To see how it sets the strength of the preference, compare two candidates. Their common denominator cancels:

wiwj=exp⁡(−Si/λ)exp⁡(−Sj/λ)=exp⁡ ⁣(−Si−Sjλ).\frac{w_i}{w_j} =\frac{\exp(-S_i/\lambda)}{\exp(-S_j/\lambda)} =\exp\!\left(-\frac{S_i-S_j}{\lambda}\right).wj​wi​​=exp(−Sj​/λ)exp(−Si​/λ)​=exp(−λSi​−Sj​​).
(3)

If rollout iii costs λlog⁡2\lambda\log2λlog2 more than rollout jjj, it receives half as much weight. Thus cost differences, rather than the arbitrary zero of the cost scale, determine relative influence. For a fixed batch, small λ\lambdaλ makes even modest cost differences strongly affect the weights; large λ\lambdaλ makes them less consequential. As λ→0+\lambda\to0^+λ→0+, the weights concentrate on the lowest-cost candidate, or split equally among tied minima. As λ→∞\lambda\to\inftyλ→∞, they approach 1/K1/K1/K. These are the two alternatives above, now connected by a continuous weighting rule.

The curves in Figure 1 show this dependence on cost and temperature. Each curve compares a rollout’s weight with the weight of the best candidate in the same batch.

The Gaussian reference already favors small controls. Its contribution to control effort will appear explicitly in the distributional objective below; SiS_iSi​ includes only state and terminal costs. The displayed weights apply when sampling from this reference, with U=0\mathbf U=\mathbf0U=0. Sampling around a nonzero plan changes how often each candidate is drawn and requires a corresponding correction to its weight.

The computational attraction is that each rollout and cost evaluation can run independently, making large batches suitable for GPU execution Williams et al., 2017. This parallelism does not guarantee that a modest number of samples will find low-cost control sequences: long horizons, many control variables, and narrow feasible regions can make the search difficult. We will check both sampling quality and feasibility when using the update in the aircraft example.

So far, exponential weighting is a rule for combining a batch of trials. To justify the rule, we need an objective whose solution gives those weights, and a reason to use their average as the next plan. Both follow by treating the candidate sequences as samples from a distribution and optimizing that distribution before fitting a new control sequence to it.

From Trajectory Weights to MPPI¶

Which optimization problem gives the exponential weights and their weighted-average update? A distribution over control sequences lets us balance low trajectory cost against a preference for small inputs. The resulting distribution need not have a simple form, but fitting a Gaussian to it produces a mean that can serve as the next plan. Sampling then estimates this mean. Throughout this derivation, randomness comes from the search over controls; the simulator itself can be deterministic.

Reference and sampling distributions¶

For a general rollout, write xk+1=fk(xk,vk)\mathbf{x}_{k+1}=\mathbf{f}_k(\mathbf{x}_k,\mathbf{v}_k)xk+1​=fk​(xk​,vk​), where vk∈Rdu\mathbf v_k\in\mathbb R^{d_u}vk​∈Rdu​ is the candidate control vector at step kkk. Collect these vectors into the complete candidate sequence V=(v0,…,vN−1)\mathbf V=(\mathbf v_0,\ldots,\mathbf v_{N-1})V=(v0​,…,vN−1​), with the same structure as the nominal sequence U\mathbf UU. The initial state is fixed, so each input sequence determines a simulated state sequence. Define the state and terminal cost of a rollout by

S(V)=cN(xN)+∑k=0N−1ck(xk).S(\mathbf V)=c_N(\mathbf{x}_N) +\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}c_k(\mathbf{x}_k).S(V)=cN​(xN​)+k=0∑N−1​ck​(xk​).
(4)

Each ckc_kck​ is the cost for one interval; if it comes from a continuous running cost, its discretization includes the interval length.

In the earlier optimal-control formulation, a stage cost ck(xk,uk)c_k(\mathbf x_k,\mathbf u_k)ck​(xk​,uk​) could penalize both the state and the control effort. Here ck(xk)c_k(\mathbf x_k)ck​(xk​) contains only the state cost; the inputs still affect S(V)S(\mathbf V)S(V) through the simulated states. Control effort will be accounted for separately by a KL-divergence penalty between the input distribution and a reference distribution.

Choose a Gaussian reference distribution P0P_0P0​ centered at zero to express a preference for small inputs. As derived below, this choice makes the KL penalty a quadratic cost on the magnitude of the nominal controls; the penalty vanishes when the nominal sequence is zero. Use a separate Gaussian sampling distribution QUQ_{\mathbf U}QU​ over complete input sequences, centered at the current plan U\mathbf UU. At each step kkk, the candidate control vk\mathbf v_kvk​ has mean 0\mathbf00 under P0P_0P0​ and mean uk\mathbf u_kuk​ under QUQ_{\mathbf U}QU​. Both use the same positive-definite covariance Σ∈Rdu×du\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{d_u\times d_u}Σ∈Rdu​×du​ for the control components at a single step. Assuming independence across time gives the joint densities over the complete sequence:

p0(V)=∏k=0N−1N(vk;0,Σ),qU(V)=∏k=0N−1N(vk;uk,Σ).p_0(\mathbf V)=\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}\mathcal N(\mathbf v_k;\mathbf0,\Sigma), \qquad q_{\mathbf U}(\mathbf V)= \prod_{k=0}^{N-1}\mathcal N(\mathbf v_k;\mathbf u_k,\Sigma).p0​(V)=k=0∏N−1​N(vk​;0,Σ),qU​(V)=k=0∏N−1​N(vk​;uk​,Σ).
(5)

Centering the reference at zero is a modeling choice. A Gaussian reference could instead be centered on a prescribed baseline sequence; the KL penalty would then charge for squared deviations of the nominal controls from that baseline. In either case, the state and terminal costs can favor controls away from the reference mean when their benefits justify the effort.

The reference remains fixed during a planning update. The sampling mean is the entire nominal sequence U\mathbf UU. This mean is taken over repeated candidate draws, with a separate mean control vector uk\mathbf u_kuk​ for each time step. Changing uk\mathbf u_kuk​ moves the center of the candidate controls at step kkk. Initializing U=0\mathbf U=\mathbf0U=0 means setting every uk=0\mathbf u_k=\mathbf0uk​=0, so the sampling and reference distributions initially coincide. Later updates can change the nominal controls at each step, moving the samples toward a new plan while the reference stays centered at zero. The sampler can therefore change where it searches without changing the reference that defines the objective.

Exponentially weighting the reference¶

Sampling from the reference determines how often different input sequences appear in a batch. Assigning a cost weight to each draw then changes how much that occurrence contributes to the weighted average. The total weight assigned to a sequence depends on both its sampling frequency and its weight per occurrence, which is why these two factors multiply.

For example, first consider a reference with only two possible input sequences, aaa and bbb, selected with probabilities 3/43/43/4 and 1/41/41/4. Suppose their costs are S(a)=λlog⁡3S(a)=\lambda\log3S(a)=λlog3 and S(b)=0S(b)=0S(b)=0, so each draw of aaa receives score 1/31/31/3 and each draw of bbb receives score 1. Their reference probabilities multiplied by these scores are

34×13=14for a,14×1=14for b.\frac34\times\frac13=\frac14 \quad\text{for }a, \qquad \frac14\times1=\frac14 \quad\text{for }b.43​×31​=41​for a,41​×1=41​for b.
(6)

Dividing by the sum, 1/21/21/2, gives probability 1/21/21/2 to each sequence. The reference samples aaa three times as often, but each occurrence receives one third of the weight, so the two effects cancel.

For continuous inputs, the same operation multiplies the reference density p0(V)p_0(\mathbf V)p0​(V) by the score e−S(V)/λe^{-S(\mathbf V)/\lambda}e−S(V)/λ at each sequence V\mathbf VV, then divides by the integral of that product:

p⋆(V)=e−S(V)/λp0(V)Z,λ>0,Z=∫e−S(V)/λp0(V) dV=EP0[e−S(V)/λ].\begin{aligned} p^\star(\mathbf V) &=\frac{e^{-S(\mathbf V)/\lambda}p_0(\mathbf V)}{Z}, \qquad \lambda>0,\\ Z&=\int e^{-S(\mathbf V)/\lambda}p_0(\mathbf V)\,d\mathbf V =\mathbb E_{P_0}[e^{-S(\mathbf V)/\lambda}]. \end{aligned}p⋆(V)Z​=Ze−S(V)/λp0​(V)​,λ>0,=∫e−S(V)/λp0​(V)dV=EP0​​[e−S(V)/λ].​
(7)

The score e−S(V)/λe^{-S(\mathbf V)/\lambda}e−S(V)/λ is not itself a probability density, and the product does not define a joint distribution of two random variables. Both factors concern the same input sequence: p0p_0p0​ specifies its density before costs are considered, and the score adjusts that density according to its cost. The normalizing constant ZZZ makes the resulting density integrate to one.

Assume SSS is measurable and bounded below and 0<Z<∞0<Z<\infty0<Z<∞. The normalized result is a Gibbs distribution: two trajectories with equal reference density and cost difference ΔS\Delta SΔS have density ratio e−ΔS/λe^{-\Delta S/\lambda}e−ΔS/λ. The parameter λ\lambdaλ has the units of cost and controls how strongly those costs affect the ratio.

The opening batch weights contain only the scores because drawing from P0P_0P0​ already accounts for the reference probabilities. Multiplication by p0p_0p0​ appears when we describe the distribution represented by those weighted samples. This explains how weighting changes a distribution; the particular choice of an exponential score is justified by the objective combining expected cost and KL divergence below.

The objective defined by the weights¶

The exponential weights solve an optimization problem over distributions of input sequences. We seek a distribution QQQ that reduces expected state and terminal cost while paying a penalty for departing from P0P_0P0​. Measure that departure with the Kullback--Leibler divergence. For densities q,pq,pq,p, it is

DKL(Q∥P)=EV∼Q[log⁡q(V)p(V)].D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P) =\mathbb E_{\mathbf V\sim Q}\left[\log\frac{q(\mathbf V)}{p(\mathbf V)}\right].DKL​(Q∥P)=EV∼Q​[logp(V)q(V)​].
(8)

This divergence is nonnegative and equals zero only when the two distributions agree. For it to be finite, QQQ must put no probability where PPP has zero density, a condition called absolute continuity. With λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 setting the cost of departure from the reference, the first optimization problem is

min⁡Q  J(Q),J(Q)=EV∼Q[S(V)]+λDKL(Q∥P0).\min_Q\;\mathcal J(Q), \qquad \mathcal J(Q) =\mathbb E_{\mathbf V\sim Q}[S(\mathbf V)] +\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P_0).Qmin​J(Q),J(Q)=EV∼Q​[S(V)]+λDKL​(Q∥P0​).
(9)

Here QQQ ranges over distributions on complete input sequences for which both terms are finite; it is not restricted to a Gaussian family.

Recall that P⋆P^\starP⋆ is the distribution obtained by multiplying the reference density by the exponential cost score and normalizing. Its density is p⋆(V)=e−S(V)/λp0(V)/Zp^\star(\mathbf V)=e^{-S(\mathbf V)/\lambda}p_0(\mathbf V)/Zp⋆(V)=e−S(V)/λp0​(V)/Z. To verify that this distribution solves the optimization problem, we can express the difference between J(Q)\mathcal J(Q)J(Q) and its minimum as a nonnegative divergence. Substituting this density into the logarithm gives

log⁡q(V)p⋆(V)=log⁡q(V)p0(V)+S(V)λ+log⁡Z.\log\frac{q(\mathbf V)}{p^\star(\mathbf V)} =\log\frac{q(\mathbf V)}{p_0(\mathbf V)} +\frac{S(\mathbf V)}{\lambda}+\log Z.logp⋆(V)q(V)​=logp0​(V)q(V)​+λS(V)​+logZ.
(10)

Taking the expectation under QQQ recovers the two terms in J(Q)\mathcal J(Q)J(Q):

DKL(Q∥P⋆)=DKL(Q∥P0)+1λEQ[S(V)]+log⁡Z=J(Q)λ+log⁡Z.\begin{aligned} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P^\star) &=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P_0) +\frac{1}{\lambda}\mathbb E_Q[S(\mathbf V)]+\log Z\\ &=\frac{\mathcal J(Q)}{\lambda}+\log Z. \end{aligned}DKL​(Q∥P⋆)​=DKL​(Q∥P0​)+λ1​EQ​[S(V)]+logZ=λJ(Q)​+logZ.​
(11)

Rearranging isolates the objective:

J(Q)=−λlog⁡Z+λDKL(Q∥P⋆)≥−λlog⁡Z.\mathcal J(Q)=-\lambda\log Z +\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P^\star) \geq-\lambda\log Z.J(Q)=−λlogZ+λDKL​(Q∥P⋆)≥−λlogZ.
(12)

The quantity ZZZ is fixed by SSS, P0P_0P0​, and λ\lambdaλ, so the term −λlog⁡Z-\lambda\log Z−λlogZ does not depend on QQQ. Choosing Q=P⋆Q=P^\starQ=P⋆ makes the remaining term, λDKL(Q∥P⋆)\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P^\star)λDKL​(Q∥P⋆), equal to zero. Every other distribution gives a positive divergence and hence a larger objective value. This proves that P⋆=arg min⁡QJ(Q)P^\star=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_Q\mathcal J(Q)P⋆=argminQ​J(Q), with minimum value J(P⋆)=−λlog⁡Z\mathcal J(P^\star)=-\lambda\log ZJ(P⋆)=−λlogZ.

The exponential cost weight is contained in the definition of P⋆P^\starP⋆; it is no longer explicit in the KL identity because we took logarithms. Writing out the density of the minimizing distribution gives

p⋆(V)=1Z e−S(V)/λ⏟exponential cost weight p0(V).p^\star(\mathbf V) =\frac{1}{Z}\, \underbrace{e^{-S(\mathbf V)/\lambda}}_{\text{exponential cost weight}} \,p_0(\mathbf V).p⋆(V)=Z1​exponential cost weighte−S(V)/λ​​p0​(V).
(13)

Multiplying the reference density p0(V)p_0(\mathbf V)p0​(V) by the indicated factor and normalizing by ZZZ is the exponential weighting introduced above. The bound on J(Q)\mathcal J(Q)J(Q) proves that the distribution constructed this way solves (9).

For a Gaussian QUQ_{\mathbf U}QU​ with the same covariance as the reference, the KL penalty is a quadratic function of its mean controls:

λDKL(QU∥P0)=λ2∑k=0N−1uk⊤Σ−1uk.\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{\mathbf U}\|P_0) =\frac\lambda2\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \mathbf u_k^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf u_k.λDKL​(QU​∥P0​)=2λ​k=0∑N−1​uk⊤​Σ−1uk​.
(14)

For example, choose λΣ−1=hR\lambda\Sigma^{-1}=hRλΣ−1=hR, where hhh is the interval length and R≻0R\succ0R≻0 specifies how costly each input direction is. Then this penalty is 12h∑kuk⊤Ruk\tfrac12 h\sum_k\mathbf u_k^\top R\mathbf u_k21​h∑k​uk⊤​Ruk​, the discretization of the control-effort integral 12∫u(t)⊤Ru(t) dt\tfrac12\int\mathbf u(t)^\top R\mathbf u(t)\,dt21​∫u(t)⊤Ru(t)dt for controls held constant on each interval. Thus, within this Gaussian family, departing from the zero-mean reference incurs a quadratic cost on the nominal controls. This accounts for control effort without adding it to SSS. Changing λ\lambdaλ with Σ\SigmaΣ fixed changes this penalty as well as the concentration of the weights.

The solution P⋆P^\starP⋆ assigns probabilities to complete input sequences. A controller still needs a nominal sequence to store and execute. We obtain that sequence by approximating P⋆P^\starP⋆ with a Gaussian whose mean can be stored as a plan.

Fitting a Gaussian mean¶

The density p⋆(V)=e−S(V)/λp0(V)/Zp^\star(\mathbf V)=e^{-S(\mathbf V)/\lambda}p_0(\mathbf V)/Zp⋆(V)=e−S(V)/λp0​(V)/Z is generally neither Gaussian nor independent across time. To approximate this distribution, consider the same Gaussian family as our sampler, with a candidate mean sequence M=(m0,…,mN−1)\mathbf M=(\mathbf m_0,\ldots,\mathbf m_{N-1})M=(m0​,…,mN−1​):

qM(V)=∏k=0N−1N(vk;mk,Σ).q_{\mathbf M}(\mathbf V) =\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}\mathcal N(\mathbf v_k;\mathbf m_k,\Sigma).qM​(V)=k=0∏N−1​N(vk​;mk​,Σ).
(15)

Only the mean sequence is adjustable; the covariance Σ\SigmaΣ at each step remains fixed. The second optimization problem chooses the Gaussian that minimizes its divergence from P⋆P^\starP⋆ in the following direction:

U+=arg min⁡MDKL(P⋆∥QM).\mathbf U^+ =\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf M} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P^\star\|Q_{\mathbf M}).U+=Margmin​DKL​(P⋆∥QM​).
(16)

Here P⋆P^\starP⋆ is fixed, and the variable is a finite-dimensional mean sequence M\mathbf MM. Expanding this objective separates the two log densities:

DKL(P⋆∥QM)=EP⋆[log⁡p⋆(V)]−EP⋆[log⁡qM(V)].D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P^\star\|Q_{\mathbf M}) =\mathbb E_{P^\star}[\log p^\star(\mathbf V)] -\mathbb E_{P^\star}[\log q_{\mathbf M}(\mathbf V)].DKL​(P⋆∥QM​)=EP⋆​[logp⋆(V)]−EP⋆​[logqM​(V)].
(17)

The first expectation does not depend on M\mathbf MM. In the second, the Gaussian normalization also stays fixed because Σ\SigmaΣ is fixed. Substituting the Gaussian log density therefore gives

DKL(P⋆∥QM)=C+12EP⋆[∑k=0N−1(vk−mk)⊤Σ−1(vk−mk)].D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P^\star\|Q_{\mathbf M}) =C+\frac12\mathbb E_{P^\star} \left[\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} (\mathbf v_k-\mathbf m_k)^\top\Sigma^{-1} (\mathbf v_k-\mathbf m_k)\right].DKL​(P⋆∥QM​)=C+21​EP⋆​[k=0∑N−1​(vk​−mk​)⊤Σ−1(vk​−mk​)].
(18)

The constant CCC collects the terms in the divergence that do not depend on M\mathbf MM. Minimizing the divergence is thus equivalent to minimizing the expected squared distance from the candidate mean to an input sequence drawn from P⋆P^\starP⋆, with distances measured by Σ−1\Sigma^{-1}Σ−1. Assuming finite second moments, differentiation gives

∇mkDKL(P⋆∥QM)=Σ−1(mk−EP⋆[vk]).\nabla_{\mathbf m_k}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P^\star\|Q_{\mathbf M}) =\Sigma^{-1}\left(\mathbf m_k-\mathbb E_{P^\star}[\mathbf v_k]\right).∇mk​​DKL​(P⋆∥QM​)=Σ−1(mk​−EP⋆​[vk​]).
(19)

Setting this gradient to zero yields the unique minimizer, since Σ−1\Sigma^{-1}Σ−1 is positive definite:

uk+=EP⋆[vk],k=0,…,N−1.\mathbf u_k^+=\mathbb E_{P^\star}[\mathbf v_k], \qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1.uk+​=EP⋆​[vk​],k=0,…,N−1.
(20)

With an exact solution of (16), the updated Gaussian would have the same mean as P⋆P^\starP⋆. The equation above identifies that mean as the quantity we need to compute; it does not yet provide a way to evaluate it. We know the density of P⋆P^\starP⋆ up to its normalizing constant: for any candidate sequence V\mathbf VV, a rollout gives S(V)S(\mathbf V)S(V), so we can evaluate e−S(V)/λp0(V)e^{-S(\mathbf V)/\lambda}p_0(\mathbf V)e−S(V)/λp0​(V). In general, however, calculating ZZZ or EP⋆[vk]\mathbb E_{P^\star}[\mathbf v_k]EP⋆​[vk​] requires high-dimensional integration, and we do not have a direct sampler for P⋆P^\starP⋆.

Importance sampling in Correcting for where the samples were drawn will estimate this mean from candidates drawn from the Gaussian QUQ_{\mathbf U}QU​, which we can sample. The normalized weights will account for the difference between the two distributions without requiring the value of ZZZ. Thus the computed update will only approximate the mean of P⋆P^\starP⋆; the equality above describes the exact target of the calculation. The quadratic example below first provides a case where this target can be calculated analytically.

Even if its mean were computed exactly, the Gaussian would retain covariance Σ\SigmaΣ at each step. It can therefore lose features of P⋆P^\starP⋆: if low-cost sequences form separate groups, their average can lie between those groups.

The first problem, (9), chooses an entire distribution by minimizing EQ[S(V)]+λDKL(Q∥P0)\mathbb E_Q[S(\mathbf V)]+\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P_0)EQ​[S(V)]+λDKL​(Q∥P0​). The second, (16), holds its solution P⋆P^\starP⋆ fixed and chooses a Gaussian mean by minimizing DKL(P⋆∥QM)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P^\star\|Q_{\mathbf M})DKL​(P⋆∥QM​). If we instead restricted the first problem to Gaussians, the identity above would give

arg min⁡M{EQM[S(V)]+λDKL(QM∥P0)}=arg min⁡MDKL(QM∥P⋆).\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf M} \left\{\mathbb E_{Q_{\mathbf M}}[S(\mathbf V)] +\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{\mathbf M}\|P_0)\right\} =\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf M} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{\mathbf M}\|P^\star).Margmin​{EQM​​[S(V)]+λDKL​(QM​∥P0​)}=Margmin​DKL​(QM​∥P⋆).
(21)

The order of the distributions in this divergence is reversed relative to (16). KL divergence is not symmetric, so these two choices of Gaussian mean need not agree Williams et al., 2017.

A one-step quadratic check¶

For a scalar system x1=x0+vx_1=x_0+vx1​=x0​+v with x0=0x_0=0x0​=0 and target 1, take S(v)=κ2(v−1)2S(v)=\tfrac\kappa2(v-1)^2S(v)=2κ​(v−1)2 with κ>0\kappa>0κ>0, P0=N(0,1)P_0=\mathcal N(0,1)P0​=N(0,1), and λ=1\lambda=1λ=1. The dynamics are deterministic: different endpoints result from trying different inputs. Multiplying the reference density by e−S(v)e^{-S(v)}e−S(v) and completing the square gives

For example, moving a scalar proposal to a positive mean makes positive inputs more common even if the target distribution has not changed. A stable finite-sample update¶

The ratio of expectations above is exact. To compute an approximate update, replace both expectations by averages over KKK independent samples from QUQ_{\mathbf U}QU​. For numerical stability, subtract ρ=min⁡iS~i\rho=\min_i\widetilde S_iρ=mini​Si​ before exponentiation. This common subtraction leaves normalized weights unchanged and avoids overflow:

wi=e−(S~i−ρ)/λ∑j=1Ke−(S~j−ρ)/λ,uk+=uk+∑i=1Kwiϵk(i).w_i=\frac{e^{-(\widetilde S_i-\rho)/\lambda}} {\sum_{j=1}^K e^{-(\widetilde S_j-\rho)/\lambda}}, \qquad \mathbf u_k^+=\mathbf u_k+ \sum_{i=1}^K w_i\boldsymbol\epsilon_k^{(i)}.wi​=∑j=1K​e−(Sj​−ρ)/λe−(Si​−ρ)/λ​,uk+​=uk​+i=1∑K​wi​ϵk(i)​.
(29)

The same full-trajectory weight updates every time slot. This ratio of sample averages is a self-normalized importance-sampling estimator. It is generally biased for finite KKK and converges to the target mean when the relevant weighted moments are integrable. Further iterations move the proposal toward useful trajectories; with exact expectations, the target mean would already be independent of the proposal.

A quadratic rollout makes the effect of this correction explicit. Take xk+1=xk+hvkx_{k+1}=x_k+hv_kxk+1​=xk​+hvk​, x0=0x_0=0x0​=0, N=10N=10N=10, h=0.1h=0.1h=0.1, and terminal cost 2(xN−1)22(x_N-1)^22(xN​−1)2. With λ=0.5\lambda=0.5λ=0.5 and Σ=5\Sigma=5Σ=5, the exact target mean is 0.8 at every time step. Sampling around uk=0.4u_k=0.4uk​=0.4 and omitting the correction instead estimates 0.88, even with arbitrarily many samples. Exercise Exercise 2 derives both limits. Moving the proposal should change the accuracy of the estimate, not the mean being estimated.

Receding-horizon execution¶

The update gives a sequence of actions for a particular initial state. Model error or physical disturbances can make the next observed state differ from the rollout prediction. Continuing with the stored sequence would ignore that discrepancy. Instead, apply only the first action and use the newly observed state as the initial condition for another planning problem. MPPI repeats the trajectory computation from that condition, as in the sampling controllers of Williams et al. (2017).

Algorithm 1 (Model Predictive Path Integral Control)

Inputs: Measured state x\mathbf xx, horizon NNN, rollout maps fk\mathbf f_kfk​, state costs ckc_kck​, terminal cost cNc_NcN​, covariance Σ≻0\Sigma\succ0Σ≻0, parameter λ>0\lambda>0λ>0, sample count KKK, and a finite number III of sampling iterations per observation.

Initialization: Set the nominal sequence U\mathbf UU to zero or to an available initial guess.

  1. At each observation, repeat the following III times:

    1. Save the current nominal sequence U\mathbf UU.

    2. Independently for i=1,…,Ki=1,\ldots,Ki=1,…,K:

      1. Draw ϵk(i)∼N(0,Σ)\boldsymbol\epsilon_k^{(i)}\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf0,\Sigma)ϵk(i)​∼N(0,Σ) for k=0,…,N−1k=0,\ldots,N-1k=0,…,N−1.

      2. Set x0(i)=x\mathbf x_0^{(i)}=\mathbf xx0(i)​=x and Si=0S_i=0Si​=0.

      3. For k=0,…,N−1k=0,\ldots,N-1k=0,…,N−1, accumulate Si←Si+ck(xk(i))S_i\leftarrow S_i+c_k(\mathbf x_k^{(i)})Si​←Si​+ck​(xk(i)​) and simulate xk+1(i)=fk(xk(i),uk+ϵk(i))\mathbf x_{k+1}^{(i)}= \mathbf f_k(\mathbf x_k^{(i)}, \mathbf u_k+\boldsymbol\epsilon_k^{(i)})xk+1(i)​=fk​(xk(i)​,uk​+ϵk(i)​).

      4. Add the terminal cost and likelihood correction: S~i=Si+cN(xN(i))+λ∑kuk⊤Σ−1ϵk(i)\widetilde S_i=S_i+c_N(\mathbf x_N^{(i)}) +\lambda\sum_k\mathbf u_k^\top\Sigma^{-1} \boldsymbol\epsilon_k^{(i)}Si​=Si​+cN​(xN(i)​)+λ∑k​uk⊤​Σ−1ϵk(i)​.

    3. Compute ρ=min⁡iS~i\rho=\min_i\widetilde S_iρ=mini​Si​ and normalize wi∝exp⁡[−(S~i−ρ)/λ]w_i\propto\exp[-(\widetilde S_i-\rho)/\lambda]wi​∝exp[−(Si​−ρ)/λ].

    4. Update all controls simultaneously: uk←uk+∑iwiϵk(i)\mathbf u_k\leftarrow\mathbf u_k+ \sum_iw_i\boldsymbol\epsilon_k^{(i)}uk​←uk​+∑i​wi​ϵk(i)​.

  2. Apply u0\mathbf u_0u0​ for one control interval and obtain the next state observation.

  3. Shift the remaining sequence one slot forward, repeat its final control to fill the last slot, and return to step 1.

This version assumes unrestricted Gaussian inputs and finite rollout costs. Nonconvex state constraints need additional treatment: even an average of inputs from feasible trajectories can generate an infeasible trajectory. Clipping samples also changes their density, so the displayed Gaussian likelihood ratio does not apply unchanged to the clipped variables. A chosen exploration covariance different from the reference covariance requires the full corresponding density ratio.

The rollouts can be simulated in parallel. Their effectiveness still depends on overlap between proposal and target. The quantity Keff=1/∑iwi2K_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/\sum_i w_i^2Keff​=1/∑i​wi2​ summarizes weight concentration: it is KKK for equal weights and approaches one when a single rollout dominates. It diagnoses sampling concentration, rather than certifying optimality or constraint satisfaction. A finite-sample update can increase the rollout cost, particularly when only a few samples carry most of the weight. Concentrated weights suggest increasing the sample count or improving overlap between proposal and target. Increasing λ\lambdaλ with a fixed reference weakens state-cost weighting, but also changes the optimization objective. Altering the proposal covariance alone requires the corresponding likelihood correction. Receding-horizon execution supplies feedback through repeated observations; the stored sequence itself is open loop.

Connection to diffusion-based planning¶

The distribution over low-cost plans also connects this computation to modern diffusion-based trajectory optimization. In model-based diffusion, the objective defines a target density through an exponential cost weight. Gaussian perturbations and cost-weighted averages then provide estimates used to refine trajectories through a sequence of noise levels Pan et al., 2024. MPPI’s weighted mean provides a useful starting point for understanding that construction. The MPPI update here uses a fixed sampling covariance and does not train a denoising network or run a diffusion noise schedule. In both algorithms, random perturbations can serve only to explore controls. Physical disturbances introduce a separate source of variation: a single candidate plan can produce different costs under different disturbance realizations. The aircraft example uses several simulated winds to estimate the cost assigned to each candidate.

Aircraft Planning Under Uncertain Winds¶

Consider an Airbus A320 flying from Montréal–Trudeau (CYUL) to Toronto–Pearson (CYYZ). The task is to choose climb, cruise, descent, and flight duration to use little fuel while arriving within 1 km horizontally and 30 m vertically of the destination. A favorable wind at one altitude may justify climbing, but its later evolution is uncertain. How can the sampled-control update account for these different possible outcomes when comparing candidate flights?

The method from From Trajectory Weights to MPPI can optimize an estimated expected cost from a simulator. It requires separate samples for candidate controls and for future winds: several winds must be evaluated before a candidate is assigned its cost weight. The following model makes those two random quantities explicit.

The airborne model and its wind state¶

In the OpenAP A320 point-mass model Sun, 2022, the state is (pE,pN,h,m,t)(p_E,p_N,h,m,t)(pE​,pN​,h,m,t): east and north position in a local map, altitude in meters, mass in kilograms, and elapsed time in seconds. Here hhh denotes altitude; numerical time steps will be given in seconds. Controls are Mach number MMM, vertical speed vzv_zvz​ in meters per second, and heading χ\chiχ in radians clockwise from north. If v=TAS(M,h)v=\mathrm{TAS}(M,h)v=TAS(M,h) is true airspeed and γ=arctan⁡(vz/v)\gamma=\arctan(v_z/v)γ=arctan(vz​/v), the model is

p˙E=vcos⁡γsin⁡χ+wˉE(pE,pN,h)+gE,p˙N=vcos⁡γcos⁡χ+wˉN(pE,pN,h)+gN,h˙=vz,m˙=−ffuel(m,v,h,vz),t˙=1.\begin{aligned} \dot p_E &= v\cos\gamma\sin\chi+\bar w_E(p_E,p_N,h)+g_E,\\ \dot p_N &= v\cos\gamma\cos\chi+\bar w_N(p_E,p_N,h)+g_N,\\ \dot h &= v_z,\qquad \dot m=-f_{\mathrm{fuel}}(m,v,h,v_z),\qquad \dot t=1. \end{aligned}p˙​E​p˙​N​h˙​=vcosγsinχ+wˉE​(pE​,pN​,h)+gE​,=vcosγcosχ+wˉN​(pE​,pN​,h)+gN​,=vz​,m˙=−ffuel​(m,v,h,vz​),t˙=1.​
(30)

The horizontal equations separate air-relative motion from wind-driven displacement: wˉ\bar wwˉ is the fixed mean wind field and ggg is a gust. Fuel flow ffuelf_{\mathrm{fuel}}ffuel​ reduces mass as the aircraft flies. The heading convention and flight-path-angle approximation reproduce OpenAP.top’s point-mass equations. Conversions to knots, feet, and feet per minute occur only when calling OpenAP interfaces that require them. The numerical derivatives are tested against OpenAP.top’s original symbolic model at climb, cruise, and descent states. Optimization itself uses forward simulation and Gaussian sampling.

The reference flight covers the complete airborne leg, with the following initial and nominal conditions:

QuantityValue
Initial mass85%85\%85% of maximum takeoff mass
Departure and arrival altitude100 ft
Nominal cruise altitude7000 m
Nominal duration3600 s

Taxi, runway operations, and traffic are outside this model. Mach number, vertical speed, heading, altitude, mass, and the geographic flight corridor have explicit bounds. Thrust, lift, and excess-energy inequalities reproduce the approximate OpenAP.top envelope checks. Adjacent command changes are also checked against limits of 0.2 Mach, 500 ft/min in vertical speed, and 15 degrees in heading. These are constraints of the teaching model.

The mean field wˉ\bar wwˉ is the committed ERA5 pressure-level snapshot for June 1, 2023, at 12:00 UTC Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), 2018. Preprocessing converts the original GRIB values once to a numerical array. The simulator interpolates in pressure, latitude, and longitude, using ISA pressure at the aircraft’s altitude. Outside the snapshot’s pressure range of 200–925 hPa, it holds the boundary value; in particular, winds near the ground use the lowest available pressure level. The snapshot remains fixed in time during a flight.

A gust observed now should influence the near-future forecast, but it should not determine the wind for the entire flight. An Ornstein–Uhlenbeck model represents this persistence and gradual loss of predictability for g=(gE,gN)g=(g_E,g_N)g=(gE​,gN​). Its exact transition over a time increment Δ\DeltaΔ is

gt+Δ=e−Δ/τgt+1−e−2Δ/τ [σE00σN]ξ,ξ∼N(0,I),g_{t+\Delta}=e^{-\Delta/\tau}g_t+ \sqrt{1-e^{-2\Delta/\tau}}\, \begin{bmatrix}\sigma_E&0\\0&\sigma_N\end{bmatrix}\xi, \qquad \xi\sim\mathcal N(0,I),gt+Δ​=e−Δ/τgt​+1−e−2Δ/τ​[σE​0​0σN​​]ξ,ξ∼N(0,I),
(31)

with τ=300\tau=300τ=300 s, σE=5\sigma_E=5σE​=5 m/s, and σN=4\sigma_N=4σN​=4 m/s. These parameters are illustrative assumptions, not estimates from the single ERA5 snapshot. The gust is spatially uniform in this example. The aircraft’s current state and current gust are observed at each replanning time. Conditional on that observation, the future gust has mean e−Δ/τgte^{-\Delta/\tau}g_te−Δ/τgt​ and increasing conditional variance. Augmenting the aircraft state with gtg_tgt​ makes this a fully observed Markov model. There is no observation filter in the example.

Expected cost under several wind futures¶

A candidate flight can do well under one wind and poorly under another. Suppose two equally likely winds give the following costs:

CandidateFirst windSecond windExpected cost
A02010
B888

Expected cost favors B. At λ=1\lambda=1λ=1, however, averaging exponential weights gives A the score (1+e−20)/2≈0.5(1+e^{-20})/2\approx0.5(1+e−20)/2≈0.5, while B receives e−8≈0.00034e^{-8}\approx0.00034e−8≈0.00034. A single favorable wind dominates A’s weight. Averaging such weights would therefore optimize a different criterion. Exercise Exercise 3 develops this distinction further.

For the intended expected-cost objective, first average costs across wind futures. If z(i)z^{(i)}z(i) specifies a candidate flight and W(ℓ)W^{(\ell)}W(ℓ) is one of LLL futures conditional on the observed gust, use

C^(z(i))=1L∑ℓ=1LC(z(i),W(ℓ)).\widehat C(z^{(i)})=\frac1L\sum_{\ell=1}^L C\bigl(z^{(i)},W^{(\ell)}\bigr).C(z(i))=L1​ℓ=1∑L​C(z(i),W(ℓ)).
(32)

Every candidate receives the same ensemble of wind futures. Pairing the winds makes each cost difference compare two plans under the same conditions, which can reduce variance in their estimated difference. The ensemble is independent of the future wind that will actually occur.

The cost CCC is fuel burned, plus quadratic penalties for horizontal and vertical arrival error and for envelope violations. Arrival error is scaled by tolerances of 1000 m horizontally and 30 m vertically. A squared unit of either scaled arrival error adds 80 kg-equivalent cost; envelope violations receive a larger penalty. The code records the physical errors separately from this combined objective.

Smooth flight parameters and their weights¶

The aircraft has three control channels over a full flight. Perturbing each short interval independently would produce a large and irregular control sequence. Instead, a candidate is a vector z∈R13z\in\mathbb R^{13}z∈R13: one duration parameter and four interior knots for each of the three control channels. The knots define small, piecewise-linear perturbations around a geometric reference flight. The nominal reference accounts for the observed state and conditional mean wind; its forward simulation remains responsible for determining the actual endpoint. The duration is multiplied by e0.025z0e^{0.025z_0}e0.025z0​ and limited to [0.90,1.12][0.90,1.12][0.90,1.12] times the nominal remaining duration. This limited family keeps the first example computationally small. It does not span all feasible A320 trajectories.

The vertical-speed perturbation has zero time integral, so it preserves the reference altitude change. This is a restriction on the control parameterization. The simulator never projects the final aircraft position onto the destination. Mach and heading perturbations can change the arrival position, and every proposal must be checked after simulation.

Use a reference p0=N(0,0.72I)p_0=\mathcal N(0,0.7^2I)p0​=N(0,0.72I) and proposal qμ=N(μ,0.72I)q_\mu=\mathcal N(\mu,0.7^2I)qμ​=N(μ,0.72I) over the knot and duration parameters zzz. The weights and proposed mean are

wi∝exp⁡ ⁣[−C^(z(i))λ]p0(z(i))qμ(z(i)),μ+=∑iwiz(i),λ=25 kg-equivalent.w_i\propto \exp\!\left[-\frac{\widehat C(z^{(i)})}{\lambda}\right] \frac{p_0(z^{(i)})}{q_\mu(z^{(i)})}, \qquad \mu^+=\sum_iw_i z^{(i)},\qquad \lambda=25\ \text{kg-equivalent}.wi​∝exp[−λC(z(i))​]qμ​(z(i))p0​(z(i))​,μ+=i∑​wi​z(i),λ=25 kg-equivalent.
(33)

The likelihood ratio is computed before the deterministic mapping from parameters to bounded duration and control tapes. Clipping the duration does not turn its physical distribution into a Gaussian; the Gaussian density remains a density over zzz. The proposal correction appears once per candidate, after disturbance averaging.

There are now two sample counts with different roles: KKK candidate parameter vectors approximate the weighted mean, while LLL wind futures approximate each candidate’s expected cost. The parameter reference regularizes the flight changes. It does not describe the physical gusts, which affect ground motion and have their own temporal dependence.

The update uses the distributional construction from From Trajectory Weights to MPPI, with C^\widehat CC as its score. Even if expected costs were evaluated exactly, fitting a Gaussian mean would not generally solve the deterministic optimization over flight parameters. The finite sampling budget introduces another approximation, so the proposed plan must be checked before execution.

Accepting and executing a plan¶

Prediction uses 60 s control intervals. Before accepting a weighted mean, the code constructs its control tape and replays it on a 10 s grid under the conditional mean wind. It checks the envelope and both arrival tolerances. The proposed plan must also improve the estimated cost on the shared wind ensemble. The best accepted plan so far is the incumbent. An invalid or non-improving update leaves that validated plan in place. The initial geometric reference must pass the same validation. At a later decision, the remaining previous plan is also replayed from the observed state and can be retained as the incumbent. Validation includes the change from the last executed command to the new first command. If neither reference is feasible, the simulation reports a planning failure.

These checks certify feasibility only under the conditional mean and at the checked resolution. The scenario evaluations expose possible arrival and constraint violations under other winds. Neither a weighted average nor a finite collection of successful scenarios guarantees feasibility for all Gaussian disturbances.

Comparing frozen and replanned flights¶

The experiment asks two separate questions: does reacting to observed wind improve arrival, and does sampling uncertain future wind improve on its conditional mean? Three execution strategies use paired physical wind realizations:

  1. Frozen plan: compute a full-trip plan using mean wind at departure and execute it for the rest of the flight.

  2. Conditional-mean replanning: observe state and gust every 60 s, optimize the remaining trip using the conditional mean gust, and execute the next minute of commands.

  3. Stochastic replanning: use the same observations and execution schedule, but average each candidate’s cost over a conditional ensemble of wind futures before updating its parameters.

The saved mean-wind flight is the validated deterministic reference used to construct the frozen plan. The two replanning variants build a geometric reference from the measured state and compare it with the remaining previous plan, then perform two Gaussian mean updates. They reuse the previous flight as a candidate incumbent, while resetting the perturbation coordinates around the new geometric reference. Within one decision, each accepted mean initializes the next sampling update. Extending the shifted-sequence warm start in Algorithm 1 to reuse the previous knot coordinates is a further computational experiment.

The realized gust trajectory has its own random-number stream. The optimizer receives only the current observed gust and generates independent conditional forecasts. All candidates at one decision share the forecast ensemble, which reduces noise in their cost differences. Controllers encounter the same underlying realized gust function even when their durations differ. Realized gusts are held over each 10 s execution interval; a 5 s replay checks numerical integration while preserving those realized inputs.

Arrival, fuel, and numerical sensitivity¶

In the three recorded wind realizations, the frozen plan misses the arrival tolerance each time. Both replanning methods arrive within tolerance in all three trials. Their fuel difference is smaller than the distinction between arriving and missing the destination, so arrival and fuel are reported separately:

ControllerFuel (kg)Arrival error (m)Feasible arrivalsLargest constraint violation
Mean-wind plan2577.866.21/10
Frozen plan + gusts2577.82491.30/30
Mean-wind replanning2587.0102.93/31.15e-13
Stochastic replanning2560.1110.03/31.5e-13

The repeated runs use 3 independent gust seeds. The figures show mean and sample standard deviation across those seeds, with individual runs also plotted. The mean-wind plan is one deterministic reference run. Prediction uses 32 candidates, 6 shared wind scenarios, and 2 updates per decision. Arrival tolerances are 1000 m horizontally and 30 m vertically. Constraint residuals and replay differences are available in the downloadable metrics.

ControllerMean ESSTotal planning time per flight (s)Rejected updates
Frozen plan + gusts11.71.30

Stochastic replanning8.852.292

Planning times are measured wall-clock times on the build machine; they include validation and vary with competing workloads. Rejected-update counts are totals across the recorded flights. The largest 5 s versus 10 s replay difference is 0.261 m in position and 0.0020 kg in fuel. All vertical arrival errors are below 8.3e-13 m.

Replanning compensates for displacement accumulated under the frozen plan. Whether sampling future gusts also improves fuel consumption depends on the wind model, the trajectory family, and the sampling budget. Conditional-mean replanning is therefore a substantive baseline. A favorable single run is insufficient evidence that the stochastic planner is better.

Increasing the number of candidate samples and increasing the number of wind scenarios address different approximations. Candidate counts of 16,32,64,12816,32,64,12816,32,64,128 are compared at L=6L=6L=6; scenario counts of 1,3,6,12,241,3,6,12,241,3,6,12,24 are compared at K=32K=32K=32. Four independent planning seeds are used at the initial full-trip decision. Each resulting plan is evaluated on 128 fresh, shared wind futures that no optimizer saw. This separates variation in the candidate search from variation in the estimated expected cost. Two projected updates need not improve monotonically with either sample count, and this first-decision check does not establish convergence of the entire feedback policy.

The endpoint comparisons in the recorded sweep are:

Costs are in kg-equivalent and include large penalties for rare unsuccessful wind futures. They are not fuel totals. In the candidate-count comparison, sample standard deviations across planning seeds are 10,00810{,}00810,008 and 7,3387{,}3387,338. Intermediate budgets give nonmonotone results, so these endpoints show sensitivity to sampling budgets without establishing convergence.

The flight diagnostics include fuel, arrival errors, fine-grid residuals, effective sample sizes, accepted and rejected updates, runtimes, and the sampling study. The local replay displays the corresponding paths and observations. To extend the experiment, increase the number of independent realized winds before drawing conclusions about reliability, and compare the gain from a richer control parameterization with the gain from more samples.

Summary and Outlook¶

MPPI begins with the single-shooting rollout and changes how its candidate inputs are combined. A reference distribution favors small inputs; exponential state-cost weights favor useful trajectories; a Gaussian fit turns the resulting distribution into a stored control sequence. Importance correction preserves the target when samples are drawn around a nonzero nominal sequence.

The aircraft application separates control exploration from wind uncertainty and averages wind costs before assigning a candidate its weight. Increasing the number of candidate controls and increasing the number of wind futures address different estimation errors. Neither guarantees that a weighted mean is feasible or improves the cost, so candidate updates are validated before they replace the stored plan.

The controller still needs an execution rule. Applying one action, observing the result, and solving again provides feedback even though each stored sequence is open loop. Receding-horizon control develops that rule further, including the choice of horizon, terminal conditions, and feasibility safeguards. These questions apply whether the planner uses derivatives or sampled trajectories.

The method’s name also reflects a connection to expectations over entire stochastic paths. Path-integral stochastic control, after stochastic dynamic programming, develops that connection and states the additional assumptions under which path weighting yields an optimal current feedback action.

Computational Sources¶

The aircraft experiments use small numerical modules and read precomputed results when the book is built. The evaluator averages each candidate’s costs over a shared ensemble of possible wind futures.

  • Gaussian importance weights and mean updates

  • Aircraft model, wind scenarios, and trajectory optimizer

  • Aircraft experiment and figure generator

  • ERA5 numerical snapshot and provenance and checksums

The experiment scripts record the physical parameters, planner settings, seeds, and validation diagnostics alongside their results. The aircraft replay displays recorded simulations without a Python kernel. Regeneration commands are in the repository README.

Exercises¶

Exercise 1 (Weights and control updates)

An MPPI iteration has scalar nominal control u=0u=0u=0, perturbations (−1,0,1)(-1,0,1)(−1,0,1), corrected trajectory costs (log⁡4,log⁡2,0)(\log4,\log2,0)(log4,log2,0), and λ=1\lambda=1λ=1.

(a) Compute the normalized weights and the updated control.

(b) Add 1000 to every cost. Explain why the mathematical update is unchanged and how to compute it without numerical underflow.

(c) Keep the corrected costs fixed and let λ\lambdaλ approach zero. Which perturbation determines the limiting update?

Solution to Exercise 1

(a) The unnormalized weights are (1/4,1/2,1)(1/4,1/2,1)(1/4,1/2,1), whose sum is 7/47/47/4. The normalized weights are (1/7,2/7,4/7)(1/7,2/7,4/7)(1/7,2/7,4/7), giving u+=−(1/7)+(4/7)=3/7u^+=-(1/7)+(4/7)=3/7u+=−(1/7)+(4/7)=3/7.

(b) The common factor e−1000e^{-1000}e−1000 cancels between numerator and denominator. Direct evaluation would underflow in ordinary floating-point arithmetic. Subtracting the minimum corrected cost before exponentiating recovers the original three weights.

(c) The unique minimum cost belongs to perturbation 1. Its normalized weight approaches one, so u+→1u^+\to1u+→1. The qualification that corrected costs are fixed matters: a likelihood correction can itself depend on λ\lambdaλ.

Exercise 2 (The likelihood correction)

Consider the deterministic rollout xk+1=xk+hvkx_{k+1}=x_k+hv_kxk+1​=xk​+hvk​ with x0=0x_0=0x0​=0, target a=1a=1a=1, N=10N=10N=10 intervals of length h=0.1h=0.1h=0.1, and terminal cost κ2(xN−a)2\tfrac\kappa2(x_N-a)^22κ​(xN​−a)2 with κ=4\kappa=4κ=4. Set λ=0.5\lambda=0.5λ=0.5 and choose a Gaussian reference covariance Σh=λ/(rh)\Sigma_h=\lambda/(rh)Σh​=λ/(rh) with r=1r=1r=1, so its KL penalty gives the quadratic mean-control effort. The proposal mean is uk=0.4u_k=0.4uk​=0.4 at every step.

(a) Complete the square in the Gibbs density to find its mean. You may use the fact that the mean of a Gaussian equals the minimizer of the quadratic in its negative log density.

(b) Find the mean estimated when the weights include the state cost but omit the reference-to-proposal density ratio.

(c) Implement both estimators and compare their mean control, averaged over the ten time slots, as the sample count increases. Does increasing the sample count correct the discrepancy in part (b)?

Solution to Exercise 2

(a) Up to a constant, the negative log Gibbs density is

rh2λ∑kvk2+κ2λ(h∑kvk−a)2.\frac{rh}{2\lambda}\sum_kv_k^2 +\frac\kappa{2\lambda}\left(h\sum_kv_k-a\right)^2.2λrh​k∑​vk2​+2λκ​(hk∑​vk​−a)2.
(34)

Its first-order condition is rvk+κ(h∑jvj−a)=0r v_k+\kappa(h\sum_jv_j-a)=0rvk​+κ(h∑j​vj​−a)=0. All coordinates of its minimizer are equal, giving

EP⋆vk=κar+κNh=0.8.\mathbb E_{P^\star}v_k=\frac{\kappa a}{r+\kappa Nh}=0.8.EP⋆​vk​=r+κNhκa​=0.8.
(35)

The result is independent of the proposal mean because the likelihood ratio cancels the proposal density in the expectation.

(b) Omitting that ratio replaces the reference quadratic ∑kvk2\sum_kv_k^2∑k​vk2​ by ∑k(vk−0.4)2\sum_k(v_k-0.4)^2∑k​(vk​−0.4)2. The corresponding first-order condition is r(vk−0.4)+κ(h∑jvj−a)=0r(v_k-0.4)+\kappa(h\sum_jv_j-a)=0r(vk​−0.4)+κ(h∑j​vj​−a)=0, so its mean is

0.4r+κar+κNh=0.88.\frac{0.4r+\kappa a}{r+\kappa Nh}=0.88.r+κNh0.4r+κa​=0.88.
(36)

Thus the two procedures converge to different expectations.

(c) A minimal implementation uses the same perturbations for both estimates so that their difference is easier to observe:

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(728)
N, h, r, kappa, lam = 10, 0.1, 1.0, 4.0, 0.5
U = np.full(N, 0.4)
for K in (1_000, 10_000, 100_000):
    eps = rng.normal(size=(K, N)) * np.sqrt(lam / (r * h))
    inputs = U + eps
    cost = 0.5 * kappa * (h * inputs.sum(axis=1) - 1.0) ** 2
    corrected = cost + h * r * (eps @ U)
    estimates = []
    for scores in (corrected, cost):
        weights = np.exp(-(scores - scores.min()) / lam)
        weights /= weights.sum()
        estimates.append((weights @ inputs).mean())
    print(K, *estimates)

The estimates approach 0.8 and 0.88. More samples reduce Monte Carlo error; they do not repair an omitted likelihood ratio. Individual runs need not approach their limits monotonically.

Exercise 3 (Stochastic aircraft rollouts and expected cost)

An aircraft simulator accepts a control sequence U\mathbf UU and a gust history WWW, and returns cost C(U,W)C(\mathbf U,W)C(U,W). The objective is EWC(U,W)\mathbb E_W C(\mathbf U,W)EW​C(U,W).

(a) A sampling optimizer generates one gust history per candidate control sequence and assigns weight proportional to e−C(U,W)/λe^{-C(\mathbf U,W)/\lambda}e−C(U,W)/λ. Explain why collecting more such weighted samples does not generally recover the intended expected-cost objective.

(b) Consider a safe candidate with constant cost 1 and a risky candidate with cost 0 with probability 0.9 and 20 with probability 0.1. At λ=1\lambda=1λ=1, compare their expected costs and their exponential scores −log⁡E[e−C]-\log\mathbb E[e^{-C}]−logE[e−C].

(c) Describe a sampling design that ranks candidate controls by an estimate of expected cost. Does this design guarantee that the weighted mean is optimal or feasible?

Solution to Exercise 3

(a) For a fixed candidate, averaging the weights estimates EW[e−C/λ]\mathbb E_W[e^{-C/\lambda}]EW​[e−C/λ], whereas the desired score depends on EWC\mathbb E_W CEW​C. The exponential is nonlinear. Favorable gust histories receive disproportionate weight, so this procedure can favor a candidate whose expected cost is larger. The reference-to-proposal correction for control sampling does not remove this difference in the disturbance objective.

(b) The safe candidate has expected cost 1 and exponential score 1. The risky candidate has expected cost 2 but exponential score −log⁡(0.9+0.1e−20)≈0.105-\log(0.9+0.1e^{-20})\approx0.105−log(0.9+0.1e−20)≈0.105. Expected cost favors the safe candidate; the exponential score favors the risky candidate.

(c) For each candidate, simulate multiple gust histories and form C^(U)=L−1∑ℓ=1LC(U,W(ℓ))\widehat C(\mathbf U)=L^{-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^L C(\mathbf U,W^{(\ell)})C(U)=L−1∑ℓ=1L​C(U,W(ℓ)). Then use C^\widehat CC as the candidate score in the sampling optimizer. Shared gust histories across candidates can make paired comparisons less variable. As the number of disturbance samples increases, this score estimates the intended expected cost. The subsequent Gaussian mean fit need not minimize that cost over deterministic plans. Finite sampling introduces further error, and an average of feasible plans may violate nonconvex constraints. The proposed plan still needs cost and feasibility checks.

Exercise 4 (Shifting a plan and checking its mean)

A controller stores (u0,u1,u2)=(0.6,0.4,0.2)(u_0,u_1,u_2)=(0.6,0.4,0.2)(u0​,u1​,u2​)=(0.6,0.4,0.2) for three intervals. After the first interval it observes a new state.

(a) Which control was executed, and what sequence initializes the next planning problem if the final control is repeated? What other input to the rollout changes at this observation?

(b) Consider the separate one-step system x1=ux_1=ux1​=u with terminal constraint x1∈[−1.1,−0.9]∪[0.9,1.1]x_1\in[-1.1,-0.9]\cup[0.9,1.1]x1​∈[−1.1,−0.9]∪[0.9,1.1]. Two feasible candidates are u=−1u=-1u=−1 and u=1u=1u=1. Is their equally weighted mean feasible? What should an implementation with a validated incumbent do if this mean is proposed?

Solution to Exercise 4

(a) The controller executed 0.6. Its shifted initial guess is (0.4,0.2,0.2)(0.4,0.2,0.2)(0.4,0.2,0.2), and the measured state becomes the initial state for every new rollout. The guess is then updated by sampling; it is not a commitment to execute all three entries.

(b) The mean is u=0u=0u=0, which produces x1=0x_1=0x1​=0 outside both allowed intervals. Feasible samples do not ensure a feasible mean under nonconvex constraints. The implementation should validate the proposal and retain the feasible incumbent when that validation fails, as in the aircraft example.

Self-checks¶

Exercise 5 (Sampling and feedback)

What makes the executed controller a feedback controller: drawing many trajectories, or conditioning a new plan on the next observed state?

Solution to Exercise 5

Conditioning a new plan on the observed state supplies feedback. A control sequence computed from many samples and then frozen still executes open loop.
